blocks.text: ‘The weirdos were taking over!’ Tate Britain relives the 1990s – in pictures
A new exhibition curated by Edward Enniful looks back on the thrilling decade before smartphones, when art, music and fashion came together with a bang

blocks.alt: Juergen Teller - Domenique, London, 29th September 1998 Tate Britain is having it’s first exhibition looking back on the art of 1990s Britain, a decade that is foundational for art and culture today. It does not attempt a definitive overview, instead focussing on setting out the ways in which art and fashion interconnected during that decade – a phenomenon that continues to this day. The 90s: Art and Fashion exhibition runs at Tate Britain, London from 8 October 2026 until 14 Feburary 2027

blocks.alt: Pendragon at The Fridge, 1999, by David SwindellsAsk Gen Z what draws them to the 90s and the answer you typically receive is: ‘no smartphones’. The 90s was the last offline decade. The internet existed, but it was slow and niche, a sparse new frontier rather than a pervasive infrastructure. Smartphones, social media, AI bots and behaviour-shaping algorithms were inconceivable. Culture was consumed in physical, analogue form, often socially. People could enjoy (or embarrass) themselves without feeling an anxious awareness that images might circulate online indefinitely

blocks.alt: Mark Mattock - Alek Wek, 1996The 90s did not resolve these tensions, but the decade did demonstrate the capacity of culture to challenge, to disrupt and to reimagine. That is the legacy this collection seeks to engage: not as a fixed narrative but as an open and evolving one.Additional text by Edward Enniful, and
